title: Game Eleven
part: PART THREE: THE HIGH AND THE HOLE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #34: Tell your goalkeeper exactly what you think of her.*

The Hawks are not like the other teams. They do not run, and they do not shout; they pass. The ball moves between their feet in a smooth, endless loop, a river that never dries up. I am still riding the high of last week, which is a problem because I told the school paper we would finish undefeated, and I meant it. I think.

Coach Brandt is in the stands, wearing a Northgate jacket that costs more than my cleats. He is watching us, though not the ball; he is watching me. He has a clipboard, and I can see his pen moving.

"Ruiz," I say to myself in my announcer voice. "Ruiz is in her element. Ruiz is the queen of Marigold Park. The Hawks are just background noise."

I take the ball, see a gap, and kick it. It hits the grass and dies. A Hawk player picks it up without running, passing it to his teammate with a touch so short and precise it feels boring, yet perfect. I am still smiling, still full of the chant. DA-NI. DA-NI. It is still in my ears, a ghost sound that refuses to leave. I think the noise is for me. I think the world is still clapping.
pages.image: Dani in a red jersey stands on a muddy field, looking confident and arrogant, while a player in a white Hawks jersey calmly passes the ball to a teammate; a man in a white jacket watches from the stands with a clipboard.

pages.text:
By the tenth minute, the score is 3 to 0. The Hawks are not fast, but they are patient, passing the ball three, four, or even five times before they shoot. They shoot once. It goes in. Four goals in ten minutes, and every single one of them came because of me.

I try to take it on myself. I run at their defender, but he steps aside, and I am too late. I kick the ball into the air, and it lands right on their winger, who scores without even looking. I lose the ball again, kick it too hard, and it sails over the bar, followed immediately by another goal against us.

I am the leak in the hull, the hole in the bucket, the reason the water is in the boat.

"And Ruiz has the ball," I say in my head, my announcer voice sounding hollow. "She is trying to be the hero. She is trying to be the savior. She is trying to be the thing that the crowd loves."

The crowd is not cheering anymore. The Hawks are passing again, the ball moving in a smooth, endless loop. I am just a rock in the stream, and the water goes around me, does not stop, and does not wait.
pages.image: Dani slides into the mud after losing the ball, looking frustrated and angry, while Hawks players in white jerseys calmly pass the ball between them in the background; the score is not visible.

pages.text:
It is 7 to 0 in the second half. The Hawks are still passing, not celebrating, not shouting, just playing with a smooth, endless patience that makes us look like we are trying to juggle oranges while riding a unicycle. They are better at this than we are. They are better at everything.

The eighth goal comes off a cross. It is a simple, perfect cross. Priya is in goal, tiny, her gloves as big as boxing mitts. The ball is coming at her. She sees it. I see her see it. She moves, but she is slow. The ball goes past her and into the net.

I turn to her. I do not think. I do not feel. I just yell.

"You're supposed to stop them! That's your entire job!"

My voice echoes across the field. It is loud. It is clear. It is cruel.

Priya stops. She looks at me. Her face is white, not pale, but the stark, blank white of a page in my red notebook that I never filled. She does not answer. She walks to the goal line and takes off her gloves. She sets them down on the grass, very gently, like they are made of glass. Then she steps out of the box, sits on the bench, and does not look at me.
pages.image: Priya, a tiny girl with glasses, sits on the bench with her back to the viewer, her oversized gloves placed neatly on the grass in front of her empty goal; Dani stands in the background, mouth open in shock.

pages.text:
Coach Gin blows the whistle, a long, sharp sound that slices through the air and, more importantly, through my pride.

"Ollie," she says, her voice flat and steady. "You're in goal."

Ollie stands up, clutching his bag of orange slices, and smiles as he walks to the box. He puts on the gloves, which are still too big for him, making him look like a kid playing dress-up with his little sister’s costumes, yet he looks completely ready.

I am taken off the field and sit on the bench, watching as Ollie faces a penalty kick. The ball is placed on the spot, the Hawk player runs, and kicks. Ollie dives and saves it.

The bench erupts into chaos. Tank is shouting, Josie is screaming, and the twins are jumping while hugging Ollie, laughing and happy. Nobody looks at me. I am invisible, a chair, a bag of orange slices, a mistake that has been corrected. The noise is for Ollie. It was never for me.
pages.image: Ollie, a cheerful boy in red, dives to save a penalty kick, his orange slice bag still in his hand, while the team on the bench cheers wildly behind him; Dani sits alone on the edge of the bench, looking small.

pages.text:
The final whistle blows on a 9 to 1 score. Our one goal was technically an own goal by the Hawks, so nobody even celebrates it. We walk off the field with our heads down. The ducks in the pond are silent, watching us go. They look like a jury that has already decided we are guilty.

In the car, the air is thick. It smells like wet grass and shame. My dad is driving. He isn't yelling. He isn't holding his foam finger. He isn't saying, "Come on, Mud Hens!" He is looking at the road. He is breathing.

My abuela is in the back seat. She is looking out the window. She says, "Even the duck felt bad for you."

I look down at my sock. I pull out the card. It says captain, and nothing else. Everything I have ever put on it, I borrowed.

The video will be online by dinner. I can feel it, already on its way.
pages.image: Dani sits in the back seat of a car, holding a small blank card in her hands, looking down at it with a sad and empty expression; her father drives in front, and her grandmother sits beside her, looking out the window.
